transcript:
# Day 21, Philosophy: The Sophists and Protagoras, man is the measure (Protagoras, c. 490 to c. 420 BC)

Picture two senior leaders in a conference room arguing about whether a product launch was a success. One points to revenue. The other points to customer complaints. Both have the same numbers in front of them. Both are being honest. And both walk out certain they are right. Who is correct? Is there even a fact of the matter, or is "success" just a word that means whatever the person using it needs it to mean?

That question is about 2,500 years old, and the first people to take it seriously were the Sophists.

The Sophists were traveling teachers in fifth century BC Greece. The word just means "wise men" or "experts." Athens was a democracy where your fortune depended on persuading a crowd, in the assembly or in court, so there was real demand for people who could teach you to argue well. The Sophists charged money for it. That alone made the old aristocrats suspicious, and later Plato made "sophist" an insult that stuck: someone who uses clever words to make the weaker argument look stronger. Keep in mind that most of what we know about them comes from Plato, who disliked them, so their reputation is contested among scholars.

The most famous Sophist was Protagoras of Abdera. His big line, paraphrased, is that man is the measure of all things: of things that are, that they are, and of things that are not, that they are not. In plain language, there is no view from nowhere. Every judgment about what is true, good or real comes from some human standpoint, and no standpoint gets to call itself the official one.

Here is the standard example. The same wind blows on two people. One shivers and says it is cold. The other, just back from a run, says it is mild. Protagoras's claim is that the wind really is cold for the first and really is mild for the second, and there is no further fact about the wind "in itself" that settles it. This position has a name now: relativism, the idea that truth depends on the perspective of the person judging.

Notice how different this is from Parmenides and Democritus, who both thought there was a hidden reality underneath appearances. Protagoras says: stop looking underneath. Appearances are all there is, and they belong to someone.

There is a practical side that matters more for a leader than the metaphysics. Protagoras taught that on any question there are two opposing arguments, and he trained students to argue both sides. That sounds cynical, but it is also what a good lawyer, negotiator or staff officer does before a decision: build the other side's best case so you are not surprised by it.

Now the objection, and it is a strong one. Plato pointed out that the "man is the measure" doctrine eats itself. If every opinion is true for the person who holds it, then the opinion that Protagoras is wrong is also true for whoever holds it. Protagoras cannot say his critics are mistaken without abandoning his own rule. Philosophers call this the self refutation argument, and most think it lands against the strongest version of relativism.

Defenders answer in two ways. Some say Protagoras was talking about perceptions and values, not about everything. The wind really is cold for you, and whether a law is just really does depend on the community living under it. He was not claiming that the number of ships in the harbor is a matter of opinion. Others say his real point was practical: since nobody has access to a god's eye view, the question is not "who has the truth" but "which view is more useful, healthier or wiser," and a good teacher helps you move toward that. Whether he held the strong or the mild view is contested, because his own books are lost.

This connects back to Heraclitus, who said the world is constant change, which makes a fixed truth hard to find in the first place. It also sets up Socrates, next in this track, who spent his life arguing against the Sophists while using many of their tools. There is a real link to the psychology track too: Kahneman's work on framing is, in a sense, Protagoras with data. The same facts, presented differently, produce different judgments in the same person.

Question for today: in the next disagreement you are in, ask whether you and the other person are disagreeing about the facts, or about the measure you are each using to judge them. Those need very different conversations.

Optional source: Plato's Theaetetus, roughly sections 151e to 171d, where Socrates lays out and then attacks the man is the measure doctrine.
